modules.title: Algorithmic foundations
modules.explanation: Count work before timing it. An asymptotic upper bound is not an exact runtime; identify the input variable and case. Geometric capacity growth makes append amortized constant despite occasional linear copies. A recursive implementation also consumes stack space.
modules.invariant: For each loop, state the number of iterations as a function of input size; separate allocated storage from returned output.
modules.tradeoff: Compare direct counting with algebraic summation; derive the recurrence rather than guessing from syntax.

modules.title: Arrays and strings
modules.explanation: Hashing replaces repeated searches with expected constant-time lookup, at a memory cost. Prefix sums turn a range sum into a difference of cumulative sums. Difference arrays batch range updates before one reconstruction pass. JavaScript strings require an explicit Unicode policy.
modules.invariant: At position i, the map or prefix table describes exactly the processed prefix.
modules.tradeoff: Compare scanning each query with preprocessing; distinguish expected hash behavior from worst-case guarantees.

modules.title: Problem-solving patterns
modules.explanation: A sliding window is justified by an invariant that can be repaired while its left edge moves monotonically. Negative numbers invalidate many sum-threshold window arguments. Binary search on answers requires a monotone feasibility predicate, not merely sorted-looking data.
modules.invariant: Each item enters and leaves the maintained state at most once; explain why moving a pointer cannot discard a valid better answer.
modules.tradeoff: Use brute force as an oracle on small cases, then prove the optimized window or search predicate.

modules.title: Linked lists and caches
modules.explanation: Pointer changes must preserve access to the unprocessed suffix. Floyd's two speeds detect a cycle without storing every node. A hash map plus doubly linked list supports lookup and recency changes without scanning; distinguish node identity from equal values.
modules.invariant: The processed prefix is valid and the unprocessed suffix remains reachable.
modules.tradeoff: Compare auxiliary arrays with pointer rewiring; a bounded cache must state eviction and recency semantics.

modules.title: Stacks, queues and monotonic structures
modules.explanation: Stacks model unfinished nested work; queues model arrival order. A monotonic stack discards candidates dominated by a later item. Its nested loop is amortized linear because every index is pushed and popped at most once. Avoid Array.shift in a hot queue.
modules.invariant: Stack entries are unresolved candidates in a stated monotone order.
modules.tradeoff: Compare scanning forward from each item with retaining only candidates that can still affect the answer.

modules.title: Searching and sorting
modules.explanation: Binary search is a boundary search over a half-open interval. Merge sort gives predictable comparison complexity and uses extra storage; quicksort needs pivot and worst-case analysis; counting sort depends on key range, not just item count. JavaScript numeric sort needs a comparator.
modules.invariant: All positions before low are known false and all positions at or after high are known true for the boundary predicate.
modules.tradeoff: Compare linear search with sorted search including preprocessing; explain stable ordering and worst-case behavior.
advanced_labs: Implement and test linear/binary search on tiny synthetic inputs; state an invariant, a counterexample and complexity.

modules.title: Trees and ordered indexes
modules.explanation: A tree traversal combines results from children according to a contract. BST validity is a global bound, not just a parent-child comparison. DFS storage depends on height, BFS on maximum width. Balancing preserves logarithmic height; serialization must preserve null children.
modules.invariant: Each recursive call receives valid bounds or returns a well-defined subtree summary.
modules.tradeoff: Compare recursive DFS, an explicit stack and level-order traversal; include a skewed-tree test.
advanced_labs: Implement and test binary trees on tiny synthetic inputs; state an invariant, a counterexample and complexity.

modules.title: Heaps and priority queues
modules.explanation: A heap exposes an extreme item without fully sorting all items. A size-k min-heap keeps the k largest seen values. Bottom-up heap construction is linear, not n log n. A k-way merge keeps one frontier item per sorted source.
modules.invariant: The retained heap represents the best k items of the processed prefix, or one frontier from each source.
modules.tradeoff: Compare full sorting with a bounded heap; account for output sorting separately.
advanced_labs: Implement and test min/max heaps on tiny synthetic inputs; state an invariant, a counterexample and complexity.

modules.title: Intervals and sweep lines
modules.explanation: State whether intervals are closed or half-open before coding. Sorting by start allows one active merged interval; resource counts use arrival/departure events. At equal timestamps, a departure precedes an arrival for half-open intervals.
modules.invariant: Completed merged intervals cannot overlap the active interval; active event count equals simultaneous demand.
modules.tradeoff: Compare pairwise overlap tests with sorting and a sweep; test touching boundaries explicitly.
advanced_labs: Implement and test merging on tiny synthetic inputs; state an invariant, a counterexample and complexity.

modules.title: Graphs and connectivity
modules.explanation: BFS finds shortest paths only with equal edge costs. Dijkstra relies on nonnegative weights; Bellman-Ford detects reachable negative cycles. Topological ordering exists only for a DAG. Union-find tracks undirected connectivity, not directed reachability.
modules.invariant: A BFS vertex is enqueued once; a topological frontier contains only vertices with zero remaining indegree.
modules.tradeoff: Compare adjacency list and matrix costs; choose shortest-path algorithms from edge constraints, not habit.

modules.title: Backtracking and constraint search
modules.explanation: Backtracking makes a choice, explores the remaining choices and restores state. A start index prevents duplicate combinations; permutations require a different used-item contract. Pruning is safe only when a branch cannot contain a valid answer.
modules.invariant: The current path is valid, and undo restores exactly the state before the choice.
modules.tradeoff: Compare exhaustive enumeration with constraint-driven pruning; output size can dominate algorithm runtime.

modules.title: Dynamic programming
modules.explanation: Define what each state means before selecting a recurrence. Memoization shares repeated subproblems; tabulation follows dependency order. Loop direction distinguishes reusable coins from 0/1 choices. For LCS and grid DP, specify both dimensions and boundary states.
modules.invariant: Every computed state depends only on already valid states and represents a complete optimum for its stated subproblem.
modules.tradeoff: Write an exponential oracle on tiny inputs, derive the recurrence, then optimize storage only after correctness.

modules.title: Greedy algorithms and proofs
modules.explanation: A locally attractive choice needs an exchange or dominance proof. Earliest finishing activities leave maximum remaining room; highest weight is not a valid replacement for weighted interval scheduling, which requires a different formulation.
modules.invariant: A chosen prefix can be extended to an optimal solution without reducing the remaining feasible choices.
modules.tradeoff: Construct a counterexample to tempting heuristics before relying on one; compare with a DP oracle.

modules.title: Advanced data structures and algorithms
modules.explanation: A trie shares prefixes while a Fenwick tree stores partial sums over bit-defined ranges. Bitwise JavaScript operators use signed 32-bit integers; arbitrary precision needs BigInt. Segment trees support more general aggregates at increased implementation complexity.
modules.invariant: Each indexed aggregate covers a precisely defined range; trie counts represent inserted words, not traversals.
modules.tradeoff: Choose advanced structures only when query/update constraints justify them; derive low-bit transitions.

modules.title: Senior engineering coding interviews
modules.explanation: Practical assessments evaluate evolving contracts, tests and maintainability, not just optimal puzzle complexity. State idempotency, error and ownership boundaries. JavaScript async I/O is not CPU parallelism; limit active work explicitly and discuss shared-state races.
modules.invariant: Every output obeys the contract even on duplicates, malformed input or partial failure; bounded workers preserve input order.
modules.tradeoff: Compare a minimal pure function with an extensible design. Refactor only after observable behavior is protected by tests.
